title: Marriage as calling
hookLine: spouses become holy through each other

lines: A WEDDING. A PRIEST IN WHITE.
cards: A Catholic wedding. The priest at the front in white vestments, the families in the pews, a cousin filming on a phone. The couple turn to each other and say their vows.
One detail: in the Latin Church's teaching, the priest isn't the one giving this sacrament. The bride and groom are. They give it to each other.

The priest, or a deacon, is there as the Church's witness, to receive their consent and to bless them. Then the reception, and home, and the real work starts the next morning, with dishes in the sink.

teach.h: NOT GOOD FOR MAN TO BE ALONE.
teach.b: At the start of the Bible, the Lord God looks at the first man and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is not good for man to be alone: let us make him a help like unto himself." Not a servant: a help like himself.
Then Paul, writing to the Ephesians, sets a very high bar: "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the church, and delivered himself up for it."
And he steps back from his own words: "This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the church." Paul's word there is mystery, and the Latin Bible rendered it sacramentum.
For Catholics, a marriage between baptized people is a sacrament: a sign that does what it shows.
The Catechism says that in the Latin Church the spouses themselves are the ministers, giving the sacrament to each other by their consent.
The Eastern tradition sees it differently: there, the priest who crowns the couple is the minister. Both are Catholic. Then the calling.
The Second Vatican Council said spouses help one another to holiness in their married life.
Not in spite of each other: through each other. The person who knows how you load a dishwasher, and how you sound when you're tired, is the one who asks you, again and again, to forgive and to give.
Every small yes counts as part of the vocation. That's the strange claim: a marriage isn't a break from the call to holiness. It's one of the shapes the call can take.

how: Catholics marry in a wedding, within Mass or a liturgy of the word, where the couple exchange vows before a priest or deacon and witnesses. In the Latin Church the spouses are the ministers of the sacrament; in the Eastern Catholic churches the priest is, and he crowns the couple.

o: a private promise that the Church simply records
a legal form the Church files for the state
a vocation where spouses grow holy through each other

o: the bride and groom, to each other.
the parents who walked them in.
games.why: the spouses are the ministers in the Latin Church. the Catechism adds that in the Eastern tradition, the priest who crowns them is the minister.

practice: If you're married, bring your spouse to mind as they really are today, not at the wedding; if not, a couple you know, maybe a marriage that's struggling, at their kitchen table.
If you pray, ask God to make them holy through each other, and name them. If you don't, hold them in mind and wish them patience, laughter, and one easy evening.

wordCard.voice: Marriage as calling. In Catholic teaching, a vocation and a sacrament in which the spouses help each other toward holiness. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, mystery: Paul's word in Ephesians 5:32, rendered sacramentum in Latin and sacrament in the Douay-Rheims.

carryVoice: Your line: holy through each other. The week ran from processions and bells to vocation and now marriage. Until tomorrow.
